briefs.label: Morning Brief
briefs.title: Michigan Operators Push Back on the 24% Tax as DEA and FDA Momentum Builds Nationally
briefs.top: In Michigan, a bipartisan wave of gubernatorial candidates is now promising relief from the 24% wholesale tax while operators like Rize and Jars find creative ways to grow anyway. Nationally, DEA's own lawyers are now arguing for Schedule III in federal court while the FDA fast-tracks psilocybin toward what could be a 2027 commercial launch.

local.text: Muskegon's Fields Cannary is targeting a fall opening for a hospitality-forward dispensary-plus-full-service-restaurant concept, pushing the retail format further than most Michigan operators have attempted.
Jars Cannabis notched a win in Madison Heights, negotiating removal of a Flock surveillance camera the city had required pointed at its parking lot as part of a 2022 licensing settlement.

Tax relief now has real political momentum on both sides: GOP gubernatorial nominee John James unveiled a "Freedom Agenda" plank proposing to cut the state's cannabis excise tax from 10% to 5%, arguing the current tax structure "drives up prices, gives illegal operators a competitive edge."

On the Democratic side, Genesee County Sheriff and gubernatorial candidate Chris Swanson has pledged to repeal the 24% wholesale tax outright, earning a public endorsement from Michigan Cannabis Industry Association Executive Director Robin Schneider, who called him "bold enough to carry the industry's message."

Not every operator is retreating: Rize, which runs three Upper Michigan locations, has sustained growth by negotiating cost-sharing arrangements with suppliers to split the wholesale tax burden — even as Higher Love closed five of its nine U.P. stores citing the same levy and a lawsuit challenging the tax's constitutionality heads toward trial.

national.text: DEA's own attorneys are now formally arguing marijuana should move from Schedule I to Schedule III in the agency's final post-hearing brief, telling the administrative court that cannabis no longer meets the statutory criteria for the strictest drug classification.

The FDA handed three psychedelic drug programs — Compass Pathways' psilocybin, Usona Institute's psilocybin, and Transcend Therapeutics' methylone for PTSD — Commissioner's National Priority Vouchers, a designation that compresses standard review timelines from roughly ten to twelve months down to just one to two months.

Compass Pathways posted six-month Phase 3 data confirming COMP360's "rapid onset and durable profile," with nearly 30% of responders reaching remission — and the company says commercial launch-readiness remains on track for end of 2026, with launch expected in first half of 2027.

Trulieve Cannabis has been approved to list on the New York Stock Exchange, executing a strategic restructuring to maintain a 100-percent-medical footprint following the federal Schedule III reclassification — a milestone signaling mainstream capital markets are opening up to plant-touching operators.

The paperwork is getting real: DEA is now sending Colorado medical cannabis businesses a detailed 26-question compliance survey — including questions like "Will you be ordering marijuana or marijuana products from other states?" — as it builds the federal protections framework tied to rescheduling.
